When doing CVD of boron carbide on freestanding carbon nanotubes (CNT) at 1000 °C, i.e., in the thermodynamically limited temperature regime, the process afforded fully conformal layer of boron carbide on the CNTs. In contrast, depositions at 700 and 850 °C afforded sub-conformal depositions. This result indicate a lower reaction probability caused by the enhanced desorption of growth species at higher temperatures.

item.title: Tunable Emission from Quasi-2D Perovskites via Electrospinning
item.description: Quasi-2D Ruddlesden-Popper halide perovskites are promising materials for light-emitting applications. They comprise corner-sharing metal-halide octahedra separated by bulky, insulating organic spacers and exhibit tunable bandgaps by varying the number of octahedral layers, n. Isolating a single n-phase within a film remains challenging, with spin-coated films generally containing a broad distribution of n phases. Their emission is dominated by the largest n-number present due to energy funneling towards narrow bandgap phases. Here, we electrospin phenylethylammonium (PEA+)/methylammonium (MA+) lead bromide quasi-2D perovskites into 140 - 400 nm nanofibers to restrict molecular diffusion. We observe progressive redshifts in absorption and photoluminescence from blue (410 nm) to cyan (470 nm) to green (530 nm) with decreasing PEA+:MA+ molar ratio. In contrast, spin-coated films with the same PEA+:MA+ ratios exhibit green emission (524 - 532 nm) across all MA+ containing compositions. Transient absorption spectroscopy reveals energy transfer within 80 ps from low n phases to MAPbBr3 domains in spin-coated films, which are absent in electrospun fibers. Electrospun fibers are also highly emissive compared to spin-coated films, with average photoluminescence quantum yields up to 77±1%. These results suggest that electrospinning limits organic cation diffusion to selectively stabilize intermediate n phases, providing a scalable route to achieve tunable solid-state emission.

item.title: Eliminating the remaining spin contamination of MRSF-TDDFT by completing its core–virtual block
item.description: We introduce a core–virtual-complete variant of mixed-reference spin-flip time-dependent density functional theory (MRSF-TDDFT), CV-MRSF, which completes the block of core-to-virtual (CV) excitations. For each CV excitation, the four determinants missing from MRSF-TDDFT are recovered by imposing exact spin adaptation, which makes every singlet and triplet spin pure and gives the proper singlet–triplet splitting of CV states without spin-pairing couplings. In addition, invariance under a rotation of the two singly occupied molecular orbitals (SOMOs) O1 and O2 adds the configurations C¹O₁²V¹ and C¹O₂²V¹. The number of CV configurations per excitation thus grows from one to four in the singlet and to five in the triplet configuration state function (CSF) response, and one quintet CSF also arises within the same CV block, instead of from a separate spin-flip-up calculation. As a result, the CV excitations properly couple to the complete set of open-to-open (OO) configurations, both singlet and triplet, as well as to the core-to-open (CO) and open-to-virtual (OV) configurations, which relaxes the excited states and accounts for most of the changes in excitation energy. For hybrid functionals, a spin-scalar one-body correction keeps the response matrix covariant under separate rotations of the core, open-shell, and virtual orbitals. For the Thiel benchmark set it lowers the mean absolute error of MRSF-TDDFT from 0.53 to 0.40 eV for the singlets and from 0.40 to 0.29 eV for the triplets. The largest gains are for n→π* states by excitation character and nucleobase singlets by molecule class. The CV block also describes the spin-pure triplet-pair states ¹(TT), ³(TT), and ⁵(TT) of chromophore dimers on the same footing, the essential requirement for the description of singlet fission processes.

item.title: Rate Theory in Chemical Potentials and without Transmission Coefficients: A Proposal
item.description: Most microkinetic models of catalytic, electrochemical, and chemical reactions neither define nor measure the transition-state theory behind their rate constants, and whether a step recrosses, tunnels, or passes non-adiabatically is unknown. This paper proposes to write rate theory for these applications in chemical potentials, so that the configurational count that a rate law assumes is explicit. It proposes, second, to write the rate in its exact form at the thermal reference rate, at which the coupling of every reactant microstate to every product microstate defines the energetic chemical potential of the transition state. This chemical potential is exact but in general not computable, and every established rate theory is a computable model of it. The transmission coefficient of a model is the correction factor from that model to the exact rate, so it belongs to the model and not to the rate law. With the transition state described by its two populations, coupled to the reactant and to the product state, mass action, Langmuir, Butler-Volmer, and the classical two-rate-constant law are special cases of the exact form. Written in chemical potentials, the treatment of the symmetry factor by Marcus and by Agmon and Levine is explicitly limited to the energetic piece of the driving force. Likewise, the Sabatier principle takes a more precise form, because an interior optimum of the overall rate of an unbranched mechanism requires a configurational or energetic excess of the transition state to respond to the binding energy of an intermediate.

item.title: Direct C(sp3)–H/C(sp2)–F Cross-Coupling of Methylpyridines with Aryl Fluorides
item.description: Direct C(sp3)–H functionalization of methylpyridines is intrinsically challenging. Herein, we report a transition-metal-free, silylboronate-mediated heterobenzylation of methylpyridines with aryl fluorides. The combination of a silylboronate and KOtBu enables direct C(sp3)–H/C(sp2)–F coupling under mild conditions, providing efficient access to structurally diverse azaarylmethanes. The reaction accommodates π-extended aryl fluorides, polyfluoroarenes, and various 4-alkylpyridines, including substrates bearing multiple potentially reactive C–H or C–F bonds, with useful levels of chemo- and regioselectivity. The method is also applicable to the late-stage functionalization of structurally complex molecules. Alkyl fluorides are also compatible via the C(sp3)–H/C(sp3)–F coupling reaction. Mechanistic studies, including aryl-halide comparison, radical-trapping, investigation of pronucleophile, Hammett plot, competition experiments, and DFT calculation support an ionic pathway involving generation of a heterobenzylic nucleophile followed by nucleophilic substitution of the C–F bond. For electronically neutral and electron-rich aryl fluorides, the observed reactivity is consistent with a concerted SNAr pathway. This strategy provides a complementary approach to conventional transition-metal-catalyzed heterobenzylic arylation and expands the synthetic utility of organofluorine compounds as coupling partners for C–C bond formation.

item.title: Multi-Agent Scheduling of Instrument-Time for High-Throughput Palladium-Catalysed Cross-Coupling
item.description: NMR time and a shared liquid-handling robot are scarce, noisy and only partially observable, so the practical question is which experiment to run next on which instrument. Existing reaction-optimisation benchmarks measure budgets in experiments rather than instrumenthours, and they learn chemical feasibility only by paying for infeasible runs. We present CHASE, a centralised-training decentralised-execution scheduler with three coupled modules: a belief encoder (PEB) infers per-instrument throughput and channel health from local event histories and exchanges only low-bandwidth summaries; a chemistry feasibility gate (CFG) masks chemically impossible actions with a four-layer compatibility graph; and a counterfactual attribution module (CFA) converts delayed campaign reward into per-step credit through leave-one-experiment-out surrogate scoring. On the Buchwald–Hartwig (3,955 reactions) and Suzuki–Miyaura (5,760 nanomole-scale conditions) HTE datasets, the ten Olympus benchmarks and a plant-wide Tennessee Eastman process, CHASE reaches 94.1% best-found yield under a shared 60 instrument-hour budget, +3.3 points over the strongest same-setting baseline, attains 90% of the attainable optimum with 25.6% fewer experiments, and cuts infeasible actions to 0.7–1.6% across plate, flow and fault-injection settings.

item.title: Quantifying the Synergistic and Antagonistic Effects of Metal–Organic Complexation on Particulate Matter Oxidative Potential via Redox Kinetics
item.description: Oxidative potential (OP) reflects the ability of redox-active particulate matter (PM) species to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) in lung lining fluid. Previous studies reported non-additive (synergistic/antagonistic) OP effects in metal–organic mixtures and attributed them to complexation-induced changes in redox potential and kinetics; however, the quantitative validity of this hypothesis remains unclear. We evaluated this hypothesis using a chemical equilibrium–kinetic dithiothreitol (DTT) assay model for the Fe–oxalate system. The model reproduced the observed non-additive interactions, indicating that the proposed redox-potential-driven kinetic mechanism can quantitatively explain these effects under the examined conditions. At atmospherically relevant oxalate-to-Fe ratios, Fe–oxalate complexation enhanced Fe(II)-driven oxidant reduction kinetics but did not produce strong synergy. Accelerated Fe(II) oxidation shifted the Fe redox balance toward Fe(III), decreasing Fe(II) concentrations and offsetting much of the kinetic enhancement. At higher oxalate-to-Fe ratios, strong antagonism arose from suppression of Fe(III)-driven DTT oxidation by weakly reactive Fe(III)–oxalate species. These results revealed that non-additive OP effects cannot be inferred from complexation-induced changes in rate constants alone, but are determined by the combined effects of reaction kinetics, chemical speciation, and metal redox balance. This framework provides a basis for incorporating metal–organic interactions into atmospheric PM OP prediction.

item.title: Risk-Priced Radio Resources for In-Line Spectroscopy and Reaction Monitoring in Chemical Plants
item.description: In-line spectroscopy now carries the chemical plant’s quality decisions over shared industrial wireless links, yet the schedulers distributing those links optimize throughput, fairness or delay and are blind to chemistry: an MIR quantification stream survives compression, while a runaway precursor confined to a narrow wavenumber window disappears with it. We present ChemRAN, a chemistry-aware orchestration framework for wireless process analytical technology networks. ChemQoI predicts how an allocation changes a stream’s analytical error, detection sensitivity and measurement-failure probability, and converts them into an expected chemical risk reduction using a sparse spectral sketch and a process cost matrix. SCARF allocates each window by marginal risk reduction under a hard safety floor for hazard streams, and RECAP couples allocation with offloading through a shared adaptation tensor and asynchronous updates conditioned on chemistry descriptors. On the Tennessee Eastman process, Buchwald–Hartwig and Suzuki–Miyaura screens and in-line MIR soft sensing, ChemRAN attains 0.9755 F1, 0.966 yield 𝑅2 and 1.08 g L−1 𝜅-casein RMSECV, cuts the risk-weighted chemical loss by 19% and the hazard miss rate from 2.31% to 0.88%, and retains over 90% of its performance on unseen plants and campaigns.

item.title: Quantum Graph-Theoretic Docking of Multiple Ligands Targeting CMG Helicase: Analysis of Interaction Patterns and Ideal Ligand Composition
item.description: Molecular docking and compound screening can overlook and biochemically relevant binding configurations of molecules, limiting the ability to identify true functional poses of potential drug candidates. To address this, we apply the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) to improve the evaluation of target–ligand interaction patterns. As a proof of concept, we focus on the CDC45–MCM2-7–GINS (CMG) helicase, which is essential for DNA replication and represents a potential therapeutic target in cancer due to mutant KRas-induced vulnerabilities in the CMG and its MCM hexameric core. In this study, docking of three ligands: methylbiocin, novobiocin, and BL_C43, to one of the ATP-binding regions of the CMG was formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem. Pharmacophore interactions were encoded in a Binding Interaction Graph and mapped to a Maximum Independent Set problem, allowing exploration of all feasible docking configurations. The quantum workflow identified ligand-dependent interaction patterns and biologically relevant binding orientations that classical docking methods failed to predict, demonstrating superior agreement with experimental biochemical outcomes for CMG inhibitors. These findings establish QAOA as a promising approach for overcoming limitations of classical molecular docking and advancing the rational design of improved inhibitors targeting CMG and other cancer-associated proteins.

item.title: Lewis Acid-Activated Bathophenanthroline Photoredox System for Chlorine Radical-Mediated C(sp³)–H Alkylation
item.description: Despite major advances in photoredox catalysis, photocatalysts capable of oxidizing substrates with Eox > +2.0 V vs SCE remain limited. Herein, we report that a Lewis acid-activated bathophenanthroline (bphen) photoredox system with ZrCl4 enables intermolecular single-electron oxidation of chloride (Eox = +2.03 V vs SCE). Under visible-light irradiation, this system promotes Giese-type alkylation of electron-deficient alkenes with a broad range of C(sp3)–H donors through chlorine radical-mediated hydrogen atom transfer (HAT). Detailed spectroscopic, electrochemical, kinetic, and computational studies reveal that Lewis acid activation of bphen enhances the excited-state oxidizing power and enables the intermolecular oxidation of chloride to generate a chlorine radical.

item.title: Tuning covalence for phosphorus-mediated C-C coupling in carbon monoxide electroreduction to multicarbon oxygenates
item.description: Electrochemical carbon monoxide reduction (COR) is a promising route for sustainable production of multicarbon chemicals from CO2, as it bypasses the large carbon losses of direct CO2 electroreduction. In most electrocatalysts currently explored to tune COR selectivity towards highadded value multicarbon oxygenated molecules, like acetate and ethanol, copper is the catalytic site of C-C bond formation. Herein, we show that by designing nanoparticles of a strongly covalent copper compound, CuSi2P3, we retain isolated copper atoms during COR and trigger the intervention of phosphorus atoms as C-C coupling sites, without directly involving copper atoms. This profound change in COR mechanism results in a high selectivity towards C2 molecules (80 % Faradaic efficiency), especially oxygenates (73%), at a current density of -150 mA cm-2. This work reveals the importance of tailoring, via the crystal structure, the local environment of metal atoms, to achieve original selectivity in COR with new families of electrocatalysts.

item.title: Polyamide Reverse Osmosis Membranes Are Less Crosslinked Than Previously Thought
item.description: Polyamide membranes are central to industrial separations, including desalination and water treatment. They are typically described as comprising crosslinked and linear units. Molecular dynamics simulations and topological analysis find branched units to be similar to or more prevalent than crosslinked units, and ignoring them can mischaracterize polyamide membranes. 2 Crosslinked polyamide membranes are widely used as selective layers in thin film composites (TFC) for reverse osmosis, forward osmosis, and nanofiltration.1 The most common desalination membranes are formed by reacting m-phenylenediamine (MPD) with trimesoyl chloride (TMC);

item.title: Mediator-Assisted Energy Release Enabled by Positional Isomerism in Norbornadiene/Quadricyclane Systems
item.description: Molecular solar thermal (MOST) systems store solar energy in metastable photoisomers and release it on demand through triggered back-conversion. Here, we show that mixtures of MOST compounds enable a distinct energy-release strategy in which one component mediates the activation of another. Using methoxyphenyl-substituted norbornadiene/quadricyclane (NBD/QC) positional isomers, we show by in situ photoelectrochemical infrared reflection absorption spectroscopy (PEC-IRRAS) and density functional theory (DFT) that substituent position shifts the electrochemical onset potential by up to 0.6 V and controls switching selectivity, largely independently of thermal stability, a trend rationalized by calculated ionization potentials. Crucially, in a mixture, the electrochemically facile QC isomer triggers back-conversion of a second QC isomer below its intrinsic onset potential, consistent with a radical-chain mechanism. Mediator-assisted triggering thus decouples the requirements for molecular energy storage and electrochemical activation and opens new opportunities for tuning energy release strategies through multicomponent MOST systems.

item.title: Enhancing Ethylene Yields and Energy Efficiency in Industrial Cracking Furnaces via Spatial Heat-Flux Optimization
item.description: Steam cracking furnaces are conventionally operated by raising the coil outlet temperature (COT) via increased fuel input, yet this approach yields diminishing selectivity gains while accelerating coking. Using a high-fidelity 3D coupled furnace–reactor model consistent with industrial design parameters, we demonstrate that COT is not the primary control lever. Instead, at a fixed total heat input, the spatial distribution of heat flux along the coil axis governs ethylene yields and cracking severity. By aligning the heat-flux profile with the axial endothermicity of the cracking reactions, relative ethylene yield increases by 5.86% while COT decreases by 3.94 K, effectively decoupling yield enhancement from fuel consumption. The causal effect of the heat-flux profile on ethylene yield makes it a more physically rigorous control variable than COT. This shifts the operational paradigm from temperature-driven to spatial heat-flux-driven control, offering a practical retrofit pathway for current industrial-scale cracking furnaces.

item.title: Mass Balance-based Computational Frameworks for the
item.description: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent anthropogenic contaminants widely 20 detected in aquatic environments. Conventional wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are major 21 emission sources that discharge PFAS via effluent and the land application of biosolids, yet they 22 are ineffective in removing PFAS. Understanding PFAS distribution and transformation in 23 WWTPs is important for the development and integration of PFAS remediation technologies. 24 However, identifying the mechanisms governing each PFAS mass flow change across a treatment 25 compartment remains challenging, and parameters quantifying PFAS transformation and 26 distribution in the field are difficult to measure. To address these problems, we developed novel 27 mass balance-based computational frameworks for PFAS distribution and transformation in 28 WWTP. We demonstrated that they are robust tools for identifying the mechanisms driving 29 changes in PFAS mass flow and for estimating unobservable parameters describing PFAS 30 distribution and transformation. Also, based on these frameworks, we found that the impacts of 31 PFAS partitioning on PFAS concentrations in the aqueous phase were two to three orders of 32 magnitude higher than those of precursor transformation. These frameworks are extensible, and 33 remaining limitations in parameter uncertainty and transformation pathway completeness are 34 discussed. 35 36

item.title: Substituted Catechols as H-Bonding Organocatalysts in Conjugated Addition Reactions of (Hetero-)Arenes to Nitroolefins
item.description: Hydrogen-bond donor organocatalysts based on thioureas, silanols, amidines and diols have been studied in-depth. However, catechols – as prototypical diol catalysts – are comparatively underexplored despite their structural simplicity, straightforward accessibility, and tunability. Here, we systematically investigate substituted catechols as hydrogen-bond donor catalysts for the conjugate addition of indoles to nitroolefins. Screening of the catechol substitution pattern identified 4bromocatechol as the most active derivative. Comparison with related diols established the importance of the vicinal arrangement and phenolic nature of the hydroxy groups. The catechol catalyst exhibits broad functional group tolerance in diverse substrate combinations. Further, the reaction was performed on multigram scale under solvent-free conditions. Combined NMR spectroscopic studies, titrations, kinetic experiments, and DFT calculations suggest a concentration-dependent association of the catechol catalyst into dimers or higher aggregates. Remarkably, 4-bromocatechol outperformed established hydrogen-bond donor catalysts. These results establish catechol as a simple, readily tuneable, and highly effective hydrogen-bond donor motif and provide a fundamental understanding of their high activity.

item.title: Accelerating Mechanistic Understanding and Prediction of Chemical Selectivity with Foundation Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
item.description: Selectivity in chemical reactions is often dictated by small energetic differences between competing transition states of less than 2 kcal mol-1. Computational predictions of selectivity for organic and organometallic reactions must reach these levels of quantitative accuracy, while simultaneously navigating the mechanistic and conformational complexity involved. Here, we assess the suitability of foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for this task. We introduce the SELECT50 dataset, a chemically diverse collection of paired selectivity-determining transition state structures, evaluated at the ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPD//ωB97X-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVP level of theory, spanning representative cases of kinetically-controlled stereo-, chemo- and regioselectivities, along with competing mechanistic pathways. We compare the performance of four MLIPs, alongside semiempirical and low-cost quantum chemical approaches, in determining transition state geometries, energetic discrimination, and pathway ordering. The Universal Model for Atoms MLIPs UMA-M-1.1 and UMA-S-1.2 predict relative transition state energies with sub-kcal mol-1 accuracy and mean absolute errors of 0.36 and 0.44 kcal mol-1, providing saddle points that closely reproduce triple-ζ DFT geometries. DFT single-point refinement further reduced the mean absolute error (MAE) to 0.25 kcal mol-1, supporting DFT//MLIP as a practical strategy for selectivity prediction. The major reaction pathway was correctly assigned in up to 98% of cases. Beyond individual transition structures, MLIPs reproduce complete organic and organometallic reaction landscapes and enable full-system treatment of selectivity-determining assemblies containing up to 211 atoms. Finally, MLIP-derived transition state energetics strongly track experimental selectivity across Ni- and Pd catalyzed reaction families (R2 = 0.87–0.90; ρ = 0.80), and with calibration, yield mean held-out MAEs of 0.12 and 0.63 kcal mol-1. Our results position foundation MLIPs as practical surrogates for the exploration and screening stages of DFT-based mechanistic analyses, enabling the throughput required for large-scale catalyst, substrate, and reaction screening.

item.title: Ab-initio Exploration of Structural, Electronic, Optical and Transport Properties of Rb2Te Photocathodes
item.description: Using state-of-the-art first-principles calculations based on hybrid density functional theory, we investigate the key material properties governing photoemission in Rb2Te for photocathode applications. Multiple crystalline phases of Rb2Te are examined, among which the α-and ω-phases are found to be both dynamically and mechanically stable. These phases exhibit exceptionally low lattice thermal conductivities of 0.27 Wm−1K−1 and 1.61 Wm−1K−1 for the α-and ω-phases, respectively. Analysis of phonon transport reveals that low-frequency acoustic and optical modes dominate the lattice thermal conductivity. Furthermore, the calculated intrinsic electron mobilities are 22.11 cm2V−1 s−1 for the α-phase and 20.91 cm2V−1 s−1 for the ω-phase, while the corresponding hole mobilities are significantly lower, at 0.46 cm2V−1 s−1 and 0.14 cm2V−1 s−1, respectively. The limited carrier mobility is primarily attributed to strong scatterings of the carriers by the polar optical phonons. This work provides microscopic insight into the electronic, vibrational, elastic, and transport properties of Rb2Te and its suitability for photocathode applications.

item.title: Contact-electro-catalytic degradation of 4-hydroxybenzoic acid using PTFE
item.description: This study introduces an ultrasound-powered contact-electro-catalysis (CEC) method for degrading 4-hydroxybenzoic acid (HBA) using polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) microparticles. Under neutral conditions, the system achieved over 99% HBA degradation in aqueous solutions. Mechanistic analysis confirms that hydroxyl radicals act as the primary oxidants. HBA degradation proceeds via primary hydroxylation and secondary decarboxylation pathway. The effects of acidic and alkaline conditions were investigated, demonstrating the non-innocent role of counter ions. Furthermore, recycling tests showed that the PTFE catalyst retains high structural integrity and consistent degradation efficiencies (96%–99%) of HBA across consecutive cycles. These findings demonstrate the potential of ultrasound-driven CEC as a robust technology for wastewater remediation.

item.title: Spontaneous Curvature and Differential Leaflet Tension Are Additive Drives for Outward Membrane Budding
item.description: Two recent models derive outward plasma-membrane budding from different starting points. Mahapatra, Malingen and Rangamani treat a microparticle as a Helfrich membrane in which phosphatidylserine exposed on the outer leaflet imposes a local spontaneous curvature over a prescribed domain, coupled to cortex linkers modelled as springs. Our own treatment derives an energetic threshold from the differential tension between leaflets generated by a net transbilayer lipid flux, with vesicle size as an output rather than an input. Here we show that the two are not alternatives: they are the two linear terms of one energy functional. Writing the bud energy with both a spontaneous curvature c0 and a differential leaflet tension ∆τ , the expression collapses—once the energy the flat reference state already carries at the same spontaneous curvature is subtracted—to the canonical form ∆E(r) = 8πκ − 4πFr + 4πΣr2, with an additive drive F = 2κc0 + h ∆τ and a resistance Σ = σ + w + KAh2/R2 containing neither drive. Budding requires F 2 > 8κΣ; the bud radius is r∗ = F/2Σ, equal to √ 2κ/Σ on the threshold locus. The additivity is exact. It is the single effective combination already known from area-difference elasticity [5, 7], written here as a force and thereby made comparable between the two treatments. A dimensionless ratio Ξ = 2κc0/(h∆τ) orders the contributions, and we exhibit a case in which each drive alone leaves the membrane below threshold, at 0.25 and 0.49 of it, while together they carry it across at 1.44 and bud at 91 nm. Evaluated with the bending moduli and boundary tensions of the curvature model, r∗ spans 41–414 nm and brackets the 45–63 nm domain sizes that model takes as input, which is a consistency check rather than a discriminating test. Retaining the KAh2/R2 term repairs the tension-free limit: the threshold does not vanish but tends to ∆ac → √ 2κ/KA/h, recovering the O(1) areadifference criterion as a derived result. We then argue that the two drives are not simultaneous—one scramblase generates differential leaflet tension transiently and spontaneous curvature persistently, so Ξ sweeps across a single calcium response, and the departing bud exports the phosphatidylserine that drove it—which makes the discriminating experiment a time course rather than a titration.

item.title: Flow-Through Capture Reversed-Phase to Hydrophilic Interaction Chromatography HRMS/MS to Expand Chemical Coverage in Environmental Non-Targeted Analysis.
item.description: Chemical coverage remains a major limitation in environmental non-targeted analysis (NTA), as conventional one-dimensional liquid chromatography (1D-LC) provides incomplete retention and separation across the broad physicochemical space of complex samples. To extend NTA coverage, we developed an online two-dimensional liquid chromatography–high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry (2DLC–HRMS/MS) approach that combines reversed-phase (RPLC) and hydrophilic interaction (HILIC) separations. Flow-through capture (FTC) modulation collects the unretained RPLC fraction using a dual-trap system combining porous graphitic carbon and trimodal reversed-phase, cation- and anion-exchange sorbents, recovering complementary sample polarity space regions within a single analysis. FTC effective transfer to HILIC was tested on a representative set of polar and mobile contaminants of emerging concern (CECs), with recoveries generally ranging from 35–100%. Feature-based NTA performance of the optimized FTC 2DLC method was compared in real water samples vs the corresponding 1D-HILIC and 1D-RPLC. FTC 2DLC yielded approximately 2.3–2.6-fold more features than individual 1D separations under both acquisition polarities. Beyond feature level coverage, data-independent componentization demonstrated that precursor-associated MS/MS information increased and was successfully distributed across both HILIC and RPLC chromatographic domains. Fragment Ambiguity Score (FAS) analysis further confirmed low-ambiguity, structurally informative fragments within the expanded separation space. Our results show that exposing the unretained fraction from RPLC separation to HILIC-MS expands the measurable chemical space and provides fragmentation information relevant to structural annotation, supporting FTC RPLC→HILIC–HRMS/MS as a promising strategy to increase chemical coverage in environmental NTA.

item.title: Head-to-tail cyclization of a peptide using a tethered homopolymer as a docking station for ring-closing and its extension to peptide cyclization and synthesis in the low bulk with mm-long tethers
item.description: A physical extension to chemical procedures for head-to-tail cyclization of peptides at the single molecule level that uses a charged homopolymer (such as polyglutamate Em with m residues) as a tethered docking station to close a linear peptide at its N- and C-ends is proposed. The homopolymer may be anchored in three ways: 1) tethering one end to a nanopore in an electrolytic cell (e-cell); 2) immobilizing one end on a fixed glass slide similar to a flow cell surface in fluorosequencing and microarrays; 3) attaching it to and stretching it between two moveable platforms in an e-cell’s cis and trans chambers, this is similar to a recent proposal for general peptide modification (doi: 10.26434/chemrxiv.15006068/v1). Multiple molecules of the target peptide containing one internal Lysine (K) residue with unprotected side chain and the N- and C-ends capped are added to trans or the flow cell. Aided by a catalyst the K residue can form a lactam bond with any of the residues of Em in trans; this docks the target onto Em. The target’s N- and C-ends are then uncapped to enable ring closing with the aid of a catalyst. Lactamization and ring closing can be detected optically, and the cyclized target cleaved from the host orthogonally. Convergence of reactants was computationally simulated at a coarse-grained level; convergence occurs in a few milliseconds. Parallel cyclization can be done with an array of Em anchors; with adequate separation, docking and ring closing can occur without cross-talk. Tethering obviates solubility issues, the purification required is minimal. The molar ratio of catalyst to target peptide in a reaction space 10 nm × 10 nm × (0.1-1.0) mm is 104-106; even though this is high virtually all of the excess products can be recovered and recycled. With small m (~30) and a 2 cm × 2 cm chip with 20 nm pore separation the maximum yield is ~1.6 femtomoles or 2.5 picograms of 1.5 kDa peptides. Scale-up can be achieved with the third anchoring method by using one platform and mm-long stretched tethers that behave like rods holding coat-hangers; long homopolymers can be assembled recursively with Native Chemical Ligation in trans followed by docking/ring-closing of peptides in cis to obtain outputs at the mg level or possibly higher. The method’s relative simplicity and low process complexity suggest its suitability for rapid construction of macrocyclic peptide libraries. With a few modifications, the method can be extended to peptide synthesis at the low bulk level. If peptide copies are situated with adequate physical separation along the tether, aggregation- and oligomerization-free synthesis of arbitrary sequences may be possible in the microgram to milligram range with only minor restrictions and without major solubility or purification issues.

item.title: Mapping Hierarchical Motifs in disorder-order transitions: learning structural motifs in supercooled liquids and crystals
item.description: Disorder-order transitions pass through structurally rich intermediates that conventional order parameters cannot fully resolve. Here, we introduce a hierarchical motif framework to characterize structural motifs from nucleation of supercooled water. Inspired by language modeling, our framework learns a discrete vocabulary and a grammar of how motifs interact in space and time. By applying vector quantization (VQ) to the learned embeddings of a variational autoencoder (VAE) trained on the structural descriptors, we establish a vocabulary of motifs comprising discrete labels of liquid, transient, and ice motifs. Moreover, the VAE quantifies local disorder that decreases from liquid to ice motifs. Analysis of the motif grammar, including motif-motif transitions, spatial co-occurrences, and ring occupancies, unifies mechanistic descriptions of the spatiotemporal dynamics of ice nucleation. The transient motifs resolve two structural roles: locally-ordered low-density (LD) environments that constitute precursors during supercooling, and non-consolidating interfacial regions. These LD precursors organize into a continuum of ring networks, revealing two processes during nucleation: trimers/tetramers continuously re-organize into closed pentamers/hexamers in ring scaffolds, while atomwise motifs relabel in bursts along an energy ladder. Next, we extend the motif framework to characterize metastable motifs formed by hypothetical polymorphs in heterogeneous nucleation simulations, which elucidates how structural motifs at the ice/liquid interface control ice nucleation. Beyond disorder-order transitions in supercooled water, we further demonstrate the generality of our framework in characterizing transitions in the nucleation of silicon and liquid-liquid transition of water.

item.title: A single reference-energy outlier nearly eliminates Co–O chemistry from a generative model's training distribution
item.description: An element-resolved audit of 44,688 oxide structures generated by MatterGen under chemical-system conditioning revealed that the aggregate composition compliance (73.27% exact match) concealed a severe chemistry-specific failure. Cobalt was omitted from 71.27% of the structures requesting it, against 8.12 ± 3.28% for the other 19 requested elements, and 98.17% of the cobalt omissions removed cobalt alone. Cell size, cation substitutability, stability gain and a general training-frequency effect did not account for the anomaly. Tracing the failure upstream showed that only one of the 8,924 cobalt oxides in the public Alex-MP-20 reference set passed the stability filter. The deficit was traced to a single anomalous reference-energy entry distorting the Co–O convex hull; excluding it raises the number of training-eligible cobalt oxides from 1 to 2,499. Four independent DFT calculations and the current Materials Project value agree within 0.024 eV atom-1, whereas the value implied by the released file deviates from them by 6.26 eV atom-1. A pre-registered intervention experiment showed that neither removal of the stability condition nor stronger diffusion guidance normalised the blind spot. These results show how a single high-leverage reference-energy anomaly can be amplified through stability filtering into a training deficit at the scale of a chemical family. Two audits that detect this class of failure without retraining are presented, namely an element-resolved condition-fidelity audit and a reference-hull vertex audit.

item.title: Layered Double Hydroxides with Interlayer Electrons Activate Strong Chemical Bonds
item.description: Layered electrides are an unusual class of materials in which excess electrons occupy interlayer regions and serve as anionic, charge-balancing species. Many prototypical layered electrides are based on subnitrides and subcarbides, motivating the search for new types of host structures. Here, we use density functional theory (DFT) to characterize a class of layered electrides derived from layered double hydroxides (LDHs). Through an anion–electron exchange process, we predict that several LDH compositions can stabilize an electride state wherein significant charge is confined in the interlayer galleries. We evaluate the thermodynamic and finite-temperature stability of the LDH electrides, demonstrating that the balance between stability and interlayer charge can be controlled through partial anion exchange. DFT calculations and ab initio molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that the interlayer electrons impart unique chemical reactivity by facilitating the activation of strong chemical bonds, such as the spontaneous dissociation of Br2 and the reduction of CO2 to formate.

item.title: Formate Electrosynthesis via Selective Ethylene Glycol Oxidation on Ni-Modified CeO2−x/NF
item.description: Ethylene glycol oxidation reaction (EGOR) offers a route to replace the anodic oxygen evolution reaction while converting ethylene glycol into value-added products. Here, electrodeposited CeO2−x//NF and Ni-modified CeO2−x/NF were evaluated for EGOR in alkaline electrolyte. Ni modification markedly enhanced the polarization response, enabling a current density of 100 mA cm-2 at 1.61 V vs RHE without iR compensation, approximately 97 mV lower than that of the parent CeO2−x/NF electrode at the same current density. During potentiostatic EGOR at 1.8 V vs RHE in 1 M KOH containing 1 M ethylene glycol, the parent and Ni-modified electrodes sustained average current densities of 192 and 241 mA cm-2, respectively. 1H-NMR analysis identified formate as the dominant detected liquid product, with estimated formate Faradaic efficiencies of 83.2% and 92.9%, respectively. These results show that Ni modification enhances EGOR activity while maintaining efficient formate formation on CeO2−x-based electrodes.

item.title: Engineering cyanobacterial carbonic anhydrase surface mutations for fast CO2 hydration and capture
item.description: Equilibration between CO2 and the other forms of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is slow under ambient conditions, bottlenecked by the hydration of dissolved CO2 to form bicarbonate and a proton. This step is often rate-limiting for aqueous CO2 capture processes under ambient temperature and pressure, and is precisely the chemistry catalyzed by the family of carbonic anhydrase enzymes. As a result, incorporation of carbonic anhydrases (CAs) into various CO2 capture schemes may be used to accelerate CO2 hydration, increasing the rates of downstream processes coupled to this DIC equilibrium. While this potential use for CA has been long-studied, extending these basic chemical principles to real applications have been hampered by practical questions of how to economically source carbonic anhydrase enzymes at mass scale. This work explores the use of modified cyanobacterial expression hosts as a potential resolution to that problem. Successful engineering of carbonic anhydrase surface display in fast-growing, marine cyanobacteria would yield a self-sustaining CO2 hydration catalyst that requires only sunlight, CO2 itself, and nutrients freely available in seawater, as inputs for passively generating carbonic anhydrases on the cell envelope during cell growth.

item.title: Synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation on microplastic and nanoplastic removal from stormwater runoff in bioretention systems
item.description: Microplastics and nanoplastics (MNPs) are emerging contaminants in stormwater runoff, posing potential ecological and human health risks. Bioretention systems offer promising nature-based stormwater treatment, yet their performance remains highly variable. Biochar, particularly post-processed biochar, has demonstrated strong potential for contaminant removal; however, its effects on MNP removal, leachate quality, and plant performance in green infrastructure remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the combined effects of untreated and thermal air-oxidated (hereinafter: treated) biochars and native vegetation (Rudbeckia hirta) on the removal of polystyrene MNPs (0.02, 0.2, and 1 μm) from synthetic stormwater runoff, leachate quality and plant performance in bioretention systems. Both biochars effectively removed nanoplastics during the early MNP-spiked storm events. Vegetation substantially reduced MNP leaching during subsequent simulated rainfall events, supported by the detection of microplastics within root tissues, indicating plant uptake. Vegetation also reduced nutrient leaching, with larger plants exhibiting more pronounced effects, highlighting the importance of enhancing plant growth for contaminant removal. Although treated biochar reduced total organic carbon leaching during initial spiking events, both biochars increased P, K, and S leaching. Overall, our findings demonstrate synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation in enhancing contaminant retention in bioretention systems, advancing green infrastructure design and sustainable stormwater management.

item.title: FAIRaman: making clinical Raman spectroscopy data FAIR through biobanking and NeXus standards
item.description: Raman spectroscopy is increasingly applied in biomedical and diagnostic research, generating spectral datasets that could support the development of robust artificial intelligence (AI) models for disease diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment guidance. However, most clinical Raman datasets remain difficult to reuse across laboratories because spectra are often stored separately from structured metadata describing the samples, their clinical context, experimental conditions, and data governance. This limits reproducibility, external validation, multicentre integration, and the development of transferable models.Here, we introduce FAIRaman, a FAIR-by-design framework and open-source software tool for the structured organisation of clinical Raman spectroscopy data. FAIRaman combines the hierarchical logic of the Investigation–Study–Assay (ISA) model with biobanking-derived descriptors for sample, donor, and processing-event annotation, and with NeXus/NXraman-inspired metadata for Raman acquisition parameters and spectral data. The resulting structure implemented in the open HDF5 file format. The software, developed in Python, converts native Renishaw WDF files and vendor-neutral text-based spectral files into FAIRaman-compliant HDF5 files through a graphical user interface (GUI), allowing users to combine batch-level metadata with sample-specific clinical data. We demonstrate the framework using a real Raman map of breast cancer tissue, and a Raman spectrum acquired from plasma-derived extracellular vesicles. These examples show that spectral data, acquisition metadata, and clinical sample descriptors can be stored within a single structured file and that the stored information can be easily retrieved using independent, freely available software tools.

item.title: Outpacing H-Phosphonate Oxidation: Enantioconvergent Deborylative Synthesis of α-Stereogenic Alkyl Phosphonates
item.description: The growing biomedical relevance of α-stereogenic alkyl phosphonates, such as their use in enhancing the metabolic stability of oligonucleotide therapeutics, motivates versatile approaches to their asymmetric synthesis. The enantioconvergent coupling of C(sp3) building blocks and H-phosphonates offers a straightforward synthetic disconnection. Herein we report the first asymmetric deborylative C(sp3)–P coupling, harnessing the synthetic modularity of alkylboron reagents to streamline access to structurally diverse, enantioenriched α-stereogenic alkyl phosphonates. Developing an oxidative C(sp3)–P coupling must contend with the susceptibility of H-phosphonates to oxidation, a property underlying their established use as sacrificial reductants in copper catalysis. We propose a twofold strategy to overcome the facile P–H oxidation: (1) kinetically favoring N–H over P–H activation to promote aminyl-radical-mediated C(sp3)–BPin bond scission and (2) incorporating a strong X-type donor into the chiral ligand to suppress Cu(II)–P homolysis. The resulting transformation combines high enantioselectivity with broad tolerance for functional groups and pharmaceutically relevant heterocycles. Cyclic voltammetry supports our proposal that an anionic pincer ligand renders Cu(II) less oxidizing than its neutral counterparts. The stoichiometric reaction of the transient Cu(II)–phosphonate intermediate with a persistent trityl radical establishes its competence for C(sp3)–P bond formation. Hammett analysis revealed accelerated coupling of electron-deficient alkylboron substrates, corroborating the design principle that increasing electron density at Cu, as achieved with the anionic ligand scaffold, promotes the oxidative coupling. Density functional theory calculations identified C(sp3)–P reductive elimination as the enantiodetermining step and attributed stereocontrol to differences in alkyl-fragment distortion energy within the chiral ligand pocket. Together, these findings establish ligand-controlled modulation of Cu redox properties and radical-trapping reactivity as a strategy for reconciling asymmetric oxidative coupling with oxidation-sensitive nucleophiles.

item.title: Disclosing the Effect of Activation on the Micro- and Meso-structure of Activated Carbons with SANS and Gas Sorption
item.description: Tuning the performance of a porous material is a major leap towards more efficient use and reduced production costs. The performance of activated carbons (ACs) in applications such as catalysis, energy storage, and environmental remediation is closely linked to their micro- and meso-structure, side to their surface chemistry. However, their intrinsic disorder and large panel of possible synthetic treatments bring to a complex structure that standard analysis technique only are not capable to depict entirely. To access a complete understanding of such a complex pore architecture, we coupled standard gas physisorption (N2 at 77 K, Ar at 87 K and CO2 at 273 K), with Small-Angle Neutron Scattering (SANS) to investigate five ACs obtained from different precursors and activation methods. By integrating gas physisorption and SANS, we obtain a coherent picture of the pore architecture and its dependence on activation strategy, revealing that the activation method governs pore structure more than the precursor type. SANS further reveals structural details beyond the reach of Ar adsorption alone by reconciling the competing models of non-graphitic carbon microstructures (i.e. curved vs flat carbon platelets) – suggesting that the balance in between models contribution depends on the activation strategy. Contrast matching with D2O further reveals that water actively modifies the carbon framework, compressing and curving defective layers. These results – relying on previous knowledge of the surface chemistry of the very same samples – provide a multi-scale understanding of structure and properties of ACs, clarifying how activation shapes microstructure, porosity and surface chemistry, with direct implications for their performance in real-world applications.

item.title: Polymorphism, Crystal Habit and Intermolecular Contact Topology in Benzothiazine Derivatives: A Comparative Hirshfeld Surface Analysis of Seven Crystal Structures
item.description: Seven deposited benzothiazine crystal structures (CCDC 1835802, 1835803, 1964377–1964379, and 2102851–2102852) were reanalysed to distinguish differences in periodic crystal structures from crystal habit and positional disorder. Eight independent molecular environments were evaluated with fragment-based Hirshfeld surfaces and element-resolved contact contributions in Multiwfn. Convergence was assessed at grid spacings of 0.20 and 0.15 Bohr and with crystal-environment clusters extending to 4 and 6 Å. In the 2018 polymorph pair, H···C/C···H contributions increase from 10.647% in 2M to 16.932% in 2O (6 Å, 0.15 Bohr), whereas H···H decreases from 40.277% to 36.922%. The 2020 deposits share closely similar major contact contributions, with H···F/F···H ranging from 24.193% to 24.600%. The two independent molecules of monoclinic CCDC 2102852 exhibit distinct H···C/C···H fractions of 19.048% and 22.066%. Alternative orientations of the disordered CF3 group in CCDC 1964379 preserve the identity of the dominant contact categories but change the F···F contribution from 3.482% (major) to 1.884% (minor at all sites) or 2.871% (minor in the central molecule only). This comparative analysis illustrates the need to distinguish polymorphism, habit, disorder and chemical substitution when interpreting contact-area descriptors; percentage contributions do not measure interaction energies.

item.title: Vinylene-Linked Covalent Organic Frameworks with Heteropore-Tuned Compact Motifs for Boosting Spin-Spin Interactions
item.description: The rich porosity of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) renders them abundant mass transport channels and easily accessible active sites. However, relatively low compact skeletons of COFs are unfavorable for in-plane and out-of-plane electron spin coupling. Herein, we report a new π-extended polyheterocyclic aromatic derivative by fusing three 2,3-dimethylpyrazine moieties to a triphenylene core, which serves as a D3h-symmetric hexatopic monomer to undergo Knoevenagel condensation smoothly with linear dialdehyde aromatics, forming a novel type of two-dimensional vinylene-linked COFs. Their three pairs of vinylene linkages at the adjacent positions of each disc-like vertex with seven fused aromatic rings tend to geometrically constrain the orientation and alleviate the congestion in the chain growth process, leading to in-plane compact Kagome motifs, alternatively patterned with the pseudohexagonal micropore and triangular ultramicropore. The as-prepared COFs enable efficient uptake of iodine molecules and generate a strong charge transfer complex at the pyridine nitrogen atoms, as revealed by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signals. The resultant radicals, densely confined in the highly ordered reticular skeletons, allow for unidirectional electron spin alignment, which further induces a typical ferromagnetic phase transition, delivering metal-free magnetism with a tunable intensity through the compacting of the backbones of COFs.

item.title: HFO-1234yf as a Source of the 3,3-Difluoropropynyl Group
item.description: Dimethyl(phenyl)(2,3,3-trifluoroallyl)silane, the defluorosilylation product of HFO-1234yf, reacts with KHMDS to form 3,3-difluoro-1-dimethyl(phenyl)silylpropyne. The mechanism of this transformation was rationalized through DFT calculations. Deprotonation and subsequent β-fluoride elimination leads to an allene intermediate. A base-catalyzed 1,3-proton migration from the allene then results in the difluoromethylated alkyne product. This alkynyl silane can undergo transmetalation with NHC-ligated Group 11 transition metal chloride complexes to form novel metal acetylide compounds with a 3,3-difluoropropynyl motif.

item.title: In-column Synthesis and Atomic-resolution Electron Microscopic Analysis of Metastable Reactive Nitrides
item.description: Metastable and air-sensitive compounds are challenging to synthesize and characterize because their formation often requires harsh conditions and their structures can rapidly evolve upon exposure to the environment. Here, we demonstrate that a high-vacuum environment inside a transmission electron microscope (TEM) column can serve simultaneously as a reaction platform and an atomic-scale analytical tool for generating and interrogating such materials. Electron-beam irradiation on sodium azide (NaN3) produces crystalline sodium nitride (Na3N) at room temperature, despite the conventional decomposition of NaN3 into sodium and nitrogen. The formation of Na3N is supported by high-resolution TEM, electron diffraction, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, which reveal correlated structural and compositional changes through irradiation. The resulting Na3N subsequently undergoes oxidation through an amorphous intermediate to form polycrystalline Na2O. The high-vacuum environment sufficiently suppresses this reaction to resolve its otherwise unachievable microscopic mechanisms. Extending this approach to potassium azide (KN3), we observe a transient crystalline phase that is most consistently indexed as K3N, a nitride known to be thermally unstable even under room temperature. Its transient appearance and decay indicate a dynamic balance between electron-beam-induced formation and degradation. These results establish in-column electron-beam chemistry as a route to metastable nitride formation while enabling multimodal characterization of highly reactive products. More broadly, this strategy offers a means of exploring nonequilibrium metastable compounds that are difficult to access using conventional synthesis and characterization workflows.

item.title: Stimulated geological CO2 reduction
item.description: Converting captured CO2 into products typically requires externally supplied electricity or H2. Although abiotic carbon reduction has been observed in water–rock systems, productive and verifiable conversion of newly supplied inorganic carbon has not been established. Here we establish stimulated geological CO2 reduction (Geo-CO2R), in which reducing equivalents released during oxidation of Fe(II)-bearing minerals drive productive conversion of supplied inorganic carbon. Natural olivine-rich rock converts supplied 13C-bicarbonate to isotope-verified 13C-formate within six hours, reaching a mass- and time-normalized productivity more than five orders of magnitude above the strongest prior olivine system. Experiments and calculations identify two mechanistic design rules: bicarbonate minimizes stoichiometric acid–base drift and sustains a productive interfacial pH window, while K+ supports greater water dissociation and a more labile interfacial hydration environment than Na+, consistent with enhanced proton-coupled bicarbonate reduction. Mineral transformation links Fe(II) oxidation to reducing-power supply, and mechanism-guided control further enhances formate production. Translating the measured natural-rock productivity using a stimulated-rock framework indicates that laboratory-scale rates could support significant, potentially commercially relevant in-situ production even when only a small fraction of the accessible formation sustains the measured activity. Upper-bound estimates further indicate a lattice-electron inventory capable of reducing millions of gigatons of CO2, equivalent to tens of thousands of years of current annual global CO2 emissions. Together, these results establish Geo-CO2R as a productive, verifiable and controllable pathway for coupling carbon conversion to geological reducing power and subsurface reaction environments.

item.title: Galvanic Coupling Links Heterogeneous and Molecular Palladium Catalysis in Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
item.description: Thermochemical catalytic reactions often consist of coupled electrochemical half-reactions, which can even serve to generate the active catalyst itself. Here we show that oxygen reduction on heterogeneous palladium drives corrosion of Pd through galvanic coupling: oxygen reduction consumes the electrons released by oxidation of Pd(0) on the same catalyst, while the soluble Pd(II) forms a homogeneous complex which facilitates benzyl alcohol oxidation. Combining corrosion measurements with quantification of Pd(II) and reaction products, we find that supplying more O2 raises the catalyst potential and accelerates Pd(II) generation and alcohol oxidation rates. Applying equivalent electrochemical potentials in the absence of O2 reproduces Pd(II) generation, and alcohol oxidation rates follow a similar dependence on the catalyst potential, which suggests that Pd corrosion is the kinetic link to thermochemical turnover. Diverting the anodic reaction to a sacrificial anode suppresses Pd(II) generation and thus the thermochemical reaction rate. Hence, O2 has two roles: it sets the potential for forming the molecular catalyst and regenerates Pd(II) after alcohol oxidation. Together, our results show that galvanic coupling provides a framework that links electrochemistry and thermochemical catalysis.

item.title: High-Throughput Combinatorial Screening of Refractory Amorphous Alloys for Fusion Capillary Systems via a Calibrated First-Principles Continuum-Thermodynamic Model
item.description: Liquid metal divertors utilizing Capillary Porous Systems (CPS) represent a critical armor technology for handling extreme heat fluxes (> 10–20 MW/m2) in magnetic confinement fusion. However, conventional crystalline refractory matrices suffer from liquid-metal-induced corrosion along grain boundaries, thermal embrittlement, and grain coarsening. Amorphous metallic alloys eliminate grain boundaries, but identifying high-temperature glass formers remains computationally prohibitive via density functional theory or molecular dynamics. Here, we present a closed-form analytical framework that couples first-principles screened nuclear ion affinities (Ai), Rose Universal Binding Energy Relations (UBER), Voigt–Reuss–Hill (VRH) elastic homogenization, Egami topological size polydispersity (δ), and Miedema macroscopic mixing enthalpy (∆Hmix) with the Johnson–Samwer Cooperative Shear Model (CSM) to predict elastic moduli and glass transition temperatures (Tg) a priori directly from alloy stoichiometry. Nonlinear least-squares calibration against an experimental bulk metallic glass database demonstrates that atomic size strain distortion is intrinsically captured by the elastic shear work (GVRH · Vm, yielding α = 0.000), while core valence charge disparity creates local electrostatic screening perturbations that enhance the shear arrest barrier (β = 0.384), reducing residual root-mean-square error by 18.5% to 41.9 K. Applying this calibrated framework to a combinatorial sweep of the quaternary Zr–Ta–Ni–Ti system evaluates 839 candidate compositions meeting CPS engineering thresholds (Tg ≥ 700 K, GVRH ≥ 45 GPa) in < 1 second. We identify Zr5Ta55Ni35Ti5 as an optimal refractory candidate exhibiting a predicted Tg = 1019.1 K, shear modulus GVRH = 67.0 GPa, bulk modulus KVRH = 178.3 GPa, Poisson’s ratio ν = 0.333, deep exothermic stabilization ∆Hmix = −30.41 kJ/mol, and robust topological frustration δ = 8.23%. This framework establishes a zero-cost computational pipeline for accelerated discovery of extreme-environment amorphous materials.

item.title: Reliability of Short Molecular Dynamics Runs as Screening Labels: Noise Ceilings, Time Dependence and Adaptive Replicate Allocation
item.description: High-throughput molecular dynamics (MD) produces the labels on which electrolyte screening and machine-learning models are built, but each label comes from one short, noisy run whose value still depends on the simulated time. We quantify their reliability, and how to spend a simulation budget given it, on HTP-MD, the largest public set of polymer electrolyte trajectories (6,137 runs of 5 ns and 133 of 50 ns). Lithium motion is diffusive in only 2 short and 5 long runs, the apparent diffusivity at a 5 ns lag is 1.95 times that at 25 ns, and the first 5 ns of a run are 1.63 times faster than its second half, biasing every short label upwards. From 94 systems simulated twice, a single 5 ns end-point label has reliability 0.47 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.63): no model can correlate with such labels much beyond about 0.69, a random forest on monomer fingerprints is indistinguishable from that ceiling (0.71), and roughly half of the run-to-run noise comes from the initial structure. A short run ranks widely different polymers well (Spearman 0.93) but not similar ones (0.68 within the screening set). In simulations with the measured noise, giving further runs only to candidates whose membership of the top set is uncertain matches four uniform replicates with 1.8 runs per candidate for the top 10% and 1.2 for the top 1%; a check on real runs is consistent but underpowered. A decision guide and all code are provided.

item.title: Radical Anion of Oxalate Esters: Electrochemical and EPR Investigations
item.description: The oxalic acid/oxalate family is an instrumental C2 platform for a circular carbon economy strategy. That molecule is the first and simplest of the C‒C bonded products obtained from CO2, and production technologies are already available, assisted by renewable electrons or from biomass. Exploiting this family of compounds as C2 synthons through reductive C‒C couplings into value-added carbon skeletons is a promising opportunity. However, the chemistry of oxalate reduction remains poorly described with the reactivity of these species under reducing conditions or the associated degradation mechanisms still scarcely investigated. Here, we combine electrochemistry, EPR spectroelectrochemistry and computational chemistry to in-depth study the electrogeneration of radical anions from oxalate esters, bringing new perspective on the degradation mechanisms of these reduced species.

item.title: Ionic router: a shared acidic pivot swaps one salt bridge for another, encoding activation state at non-homologous positions in class B1 and class A GPCRs
item.description: We report the first instance in a class B1 G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) of a charged residue that exchanges one state-specific salt bridge for another, and the first evidence that this arrangement recurs at non-homologous positions in two receptor classes. In the human glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R), E408, generic number 8.49x49, pairs with R348 (6.37x37) in 5 of 5 scorable inactive structures and 0 of 52 active, and with R176 (2.46x46) in 42 of 52 active structures and 0 of 6 inactive. Across all fifteen class B1 receptors, the bond to 6.37x37 is absent from all 131 scorable active structures and the bond to 2.46x46 is present in 97 of 135, so the active-state arrangement holds family-wide; the exchange requires both states, and only GLP-1R carries enough inactive structures to show it. These three positions, together with a fourth at 8.47x47, have been described as a cytoplasmic polar network that holds the receptor inactive and breaks on activation, releasing its residues, a reading carried from homology models and mutagenesis through the first activated structure of the receptor to ligand-free G protein complexes of three class B1 receptors in 2024 and to a clinical report in the parathyroid hormone receptor in 2026 [1-7]. Release predicts that the pivot ends the transition bound to fewer partners. It does not: the number of salt bridges it makes does not change across the transition, only the identity of its partner. The inactive-state bond does break, as reported. The pivot is not released: it takes a second partner that is carried only in the active state. We name this arrangement an ionic router. An ionic router is a charged residue that exchanges salt-bridge partners between two conformational states: in each state it binds at least one oppositely charged partner that it does not bind in the other. Each arm is itself a lock, and the two are mutually exclusive: one is closed in each state, so the pivot is never free. The arrangement was found by an unbiased screen that ranked 2,257 charged positions across 61 receptors, scored only on the separation between partner-identity change and partner-count change. No measure of this form is reported in the literature, and a measure that scores one contact at a time cannot separate an exchange from a loss. The screen places the GLP-1R position first of 48 rankable positions in that receptor. Without reference to that result, it places the equivalent class A arrangement first of 38 rankable charged positions in bovine rhodopsin, recovering the exchange at E247 (6.30x30) between R135 (3.50x50) and K231 (5.66x66), partners that never contact one another in any structure. Prior reports describe the class A exchange from the ligand-free opsin structures, from NMR and from simulation [8-12], and propose an equivalent contact in the adenosine receptors from simulation [13, 14]. Recovering a documented arrangement without being directed at it is the control on the measure, and the measure then finds the class B1 instance at positions already described, where it reverses the direction assigned to them. It is the first such arrangement reported outside class A. The class A pairing could not have been used in GLP-1R: all fifteen class B1 receptors carry a glutamate where class A carries the arginine at 3.50x50, and that position is occupied instead by a histidine contact present in both states. A single side chain that registers activation state by which partner it holds is a candidate site for precision drug design and for understanding the molecular basis of disease.

item.title: Low-Energy Electron Attachment to Catechin Sulphate
item.description: Low-energy electron (LEE) attachment can initiate molecular fragmentation through temporary negative ion states, with autodetachment competing against nuclear motion toward dissociation. Here, we apply an improved local complex potential time-dependent wavepacket (LCP-TDWP) workflow to catechin sulphate, a metabolically relevant catechin conjugate for which, to our knowledge, a dedicated dissociative electron attachment (DEA) study has not been reported. The present model follows one C–O bond extension coordinate selected for cleavage leading to a C5-centered catechin-derived radical and the stable bisulfate anion, HSO_{4}^{-} . Neutral and anionic potential energy curves were calculated at the CAM-B3LYP/6-311++G(2d,2p) level, and vibrational eigenfunctions were obtained with the Fourier grid Hamiltonian method. A phenomenological coordinate-dependent width was constructed from an exponential envelope centered at the Franck–Condon coordinate, a Wigner-type energy factor based on the local anion–neutral energy difference, and a smooth switch near the curve crossing; its parameters were not benchmarked against an independent stabilization or CAP-EOM-EA width calculation. Propagation used a symmetric split operator with a 0.1000 fs time step for 1.000 ps and a complex absorbing potential (CAP) beginning at 7.250 a0. The neutral Franck–Condon coordinate and first relevant curve crossing are 2.659 and 3.327 a0, respectively, and the modeled width reaches 0.03434 eV. The autocorrelation spectrum has a doorway feature near 0.4512 eV, whereas the calculated DEA cross section peaks at 1.113 eV with a maximum of 4.608 Mb. The cumulative CAP loss from the initial packet at 1.000 ps is 0.003162 (0.3162%); this value is not a branching fraction or an experimentally measured DEA yield. These results provide a methodological basis for analyzing competition between autodetachment and a selected dissociation channel.

item.title: When Can an Off-Cycle Reservoir Raise a Catalyst’s Turnover Number?
item.description: Off-cycle species are typically considered detrimental to catalytic activity; however, a dormant form can also extend catalyst lifetime. This study shows under which conditions a reversible off-cycle reservoir can increase the turnover number (TON) of a homogeneous catalyst. When both turnover and all deactivation steps are first order in catalyst, branching remains constant over time and the reservoir only holds the catalyst in a dormant state, the distribution of turnovers per catalyst does not change, regardless of the number of reservoirs. The reaction is slowed, and under an external clock, such as a poison that forms independently of the catalyst, the TON decreases. When deactivation is of higher order in catalyst than turnover, a fast reservoir of depth acts as a -fold dilution. This increases the TON up to a ceiling set by the first-order deactivation pathways, and for a given batch time there is an optimal depth. In the published model of (DTBM-SEGPHOS)CuH, the HBpin adduct protects the catalyst from aggregation but is 2.9–5.9 times deeper than optimal. In Hoveyda–Grubbs metathesis, a styrenyl-ether reservoir slows the reaction threefold without reducing the TON. A reservoir can be beneficial only if the catalyst-limited TON decreases as catalyst loading increases, that is, if the slope of log TON against log loading is negative. Dilution experiments and a series with graded amounts of additive then show whether it will be.

item.title: Ice Deposition of Water Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry at Cryogenic Temperatures
item.description: Water gas cluster ion beams (GCIBs) are increasingly used in cryogenic secondary ion mass spectrometry (cryo-SIMS) to improve the detection of biomolecules while preserving their molecular integrity. However, the effects of water cluster primary ion (PI) beams on cryogenically cooled surfaces are not yet fully understood. Here, we demonstrate that continuous bombardment with (H2O)n+ GCIBs can induce ice deposition, which competes with sputtering and can ultimately obscure the underlying sample, thus compromising depth profiling and molecular analysis. Using deuterated (D2O)n+ clusters and subsequent C60+ depth profiling, we confirmed that the deposited ice originates predominantly from water molecules introduced by the primary ion beam. Systematic investigation of cluster size and kinetic energy identified the energy per water molecule (E/n) as the key parameter governing the balance between net sputtering and ice deposition. Significant ice deposition occurred at E/n < 4 eV, whereas the substrate signal remained approximately constant at E/n > 5 eV. Measurements of the deposited ice cross-sections indicated that up to 40% of the incoming water molecules could remain on the surface under deposition-dominated conditions. Substrate temperature also influenced deposition, with ice accumulation observed below approximately 188 K for the investigated beam conditions. Experiments on copper, organic deposits, and mouse brain tissue further demonstrated that this phenomenon is not restricted to metallic substrates and that the deposition rate varies with surface composition. These findings establish beam energy per molecule, substrate temperature, and material-dependent sputtering behaviour as important factors controlling ice accumulation during cryo-SIMS using (H2O)n+ GCIBs. Careful optimisation of GCIB parameters is therefore essential to minimise deposition artefacts and maintain reliable molecular depth profiling, particularly when cryogenic sample preservation is required. Lastly, the ability to deposit known amounts of ice in localised areas could prove useful for preparing samples with well-defined and controlled characteristics.

item.title: Patterning Conductive Aluminium onto Temperature Sensitive Polymers and Tattoo Paper at Room Temperature and Pressure
item.description: Currently patterning conductive metal onto thermally fragile substrates remains hindered by the necessary processing conditions required. Aluminium is an attractive conductor for printed electronics, being non-toxic, low cost, having high abundance, while providing excellent electrical conductivity. Here, we report the direct deposition of conductive aluminium lines onto a selection of heat sensitive substrates; namely dissolvable tattoo paper, and a Polyborosiloxane (PBS)/Sylgard blend substrate at room temperature and atmospheric pressure using an atmospheric-pressure plasma jet (APPJ) and an ethereal solution of dimethylethylamine alane (DMEAA) as a metal-organic precursor ink. Unlike conventional metal-organic decomposition methods that require thermal post-treatment, the non-equilibrium plasma drives precursor fragmentation, ligand removal, and metallic film formation in a single step without external substrate heating. Optimised tracks were produced on dissolvable tattoo paper yielding a best sheet resistance of 1.59 ± 0.64 kΩ/sq due to its metallic nature. The tracks were deposited directly onto dissolvable tattoo paper, and sufficiently conductive to complete a functional electrical circuit allowing it to be transferred to skin, demonstrating a viable route to low-temperature aluminium metallisation on porous substrates.

item.title: Dynamic Anionic Speciation and Proton Transfer in Choline/Geranic Acid Mixtures Revealed by Machine-Learned Molecular Dynamics
item.description: In carboxylate/carboxylic acid-containing ionic liquid systems, oligomeric complex anions have been shown to substantially alter transport properties; yet whether such persistent pairing survives in the presence of water remains an open question. The 1:2 choline/geranic acid mixture (CAGE12) provides an ideal case study: a promising therapeutic solvent unavoidably hydrated in biomedical use. Although hydrogen-bonded geranic acid (AGE)–geranate (GE) oligomeric motifs have been proposed and recently characterized spectroscopically, their prevalence and dynamical relevance in the liquid remain unclear, particularly in application conditions. Here, we employ DFT-trained NeuralIL machine-learned molecular dynamics to investigate hydrated CAGE12 containing 8 wt% water. The simulations reveal a highly dynamic hydrogen-bond network centered on GE, in which AGE, water, and choline continuously compete for coordinating the GE. AGE–GE associations are frequently observed but exhibit sub-picosecond lifetimes, indicating that they are transient structural motifs rather than persistent complex anions. Proton-transferred configurations are found to depend strongly on the local hydrogen-bond environment. Rare AGE-rich coordination environments are associated with proton-transferred configurations that remain stable, whereas the more abundant water-coordinated AGE–GE pairs are associated with reversible proton-transfer events and proton rattling. Overall, hydrated CAGE12 is best described as a dynamically evolving hydrogen-bond network in which transient local coordination, rather than persistent oligomeric anions, governs proton transfer and anionic speciation. These results highlight the critical role of water in disrupting complex anion formation in nonstoichiometric ionic liquids, with direct consequences for their transport and physicochemical properties.

item.title: Mechanochemically Accelerated Defluorosilylation of α-Trifluoromethyl Styrenes
item.description: We report a mechanochemical copper-catalyzed defluorosilylation of α-trifluoromethyl styrenes with silylboranes. Mechanical activation dramatically accelerated the C–F bond transformation, reducing the reaction time from 8 h to only 30 min at room temperature while substantially decreasing solvent consumption. The reaction exhibits broad substrate compatibility and scalability, highlighting mechanochemistry as an effective strategy for accelerating selective C–F bond functionalization.

item.title: Two-photon-enabled near-infrared proximity labeling maps protein neighborhoods in vivo
item.description: Native molecular neighborhoods govern biological processes and disease, yet existing approaches trade off penetration, precision, and native compatibility. Photocatalytic proximity labeling (PL) offers nanoscale, genetics-free precision but is limited by visible-light activation in optically opaque tissue. Here, we report 2PMap, a two-photon near-infrared PL platform driven by a sensitizer with a twophoton absorption cross-section nearly two orders of magnitude above conventional photocatalysts, enabling 850 nm continuous-wave excitation without pulsed lasers. In optically opaque samples, 2PMap achieved higher proteome coverage than conventional visible-light PL. In an early-stage Alzheimer’s disease mouse model, peptide-guided 2PMap produced the first proximity scale map of connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) in living brain tissue, capturing an 80-node network spanning extracellular-matrix, vascular, immune, and neuronal components within a microenvironment inaccessible to existing PL methods. 2PMap thus provides a genetics-free, modular platform for spatial proteomic mapping, extending molecular cartography to previously inaccessible living systems.

item.title: Morgan Fingerprint Classification Prioritizes Autophagy Modulators While Transcriptome Regression Fails to Distinguish Opposing Modulators
item.description: Autophagy is a conserved lysosomal degradation and recycling pathway with established roles in aging, neurodegeneration, cancer, and metabolic disease. Computational prioritization of autophagy modulators is difficult: autophagy modulators have a variety of mechanisms and the analysis of perturbational transcriptomes could confound pathway-specific effects with generic stress responses. Here, we evaluated four formulations of the prioritization task: full transcriptome regression, gene-signature matching, binary modulator classification, and activator-versus-inhibitor direction prediction, using LINCS L1000 transcriptomics, the Human Autophagy Modulator Database (HAMdb), and a 99,433-compound ChEMBL library. We found that a Uni-Mol neural network trained to predict 12,328-gene expression responses assigned near-identical profiles to Rapamycin and Wortmannin, two compounds with opposing effects on autophagy (predicted Spearman ρ = +0.97 versus +0.43 observed), and that genome-wide diagnostics detected no association between molecular structure and expression. In contrast, XGBoost on 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints distinguished modulators from non-modulators with compound-level AUROC 0.845 using L1000 context and 0.84 to 0.88 (95% bootstrap CI) from structure alone, ranking held-out canonical controls at the top of the score distribution, and enriched autophagy and mTOR/PI3K annotations up to ~36× and ~58× over baseline on the ChEMBL library.
